content: Why can an application still feel slow after its database search becomes quick? I thought adding an index speeds every query, so the whole request should become fast once that shortcut is available.

An index can shorten the database portion without changing the rest of the request. The application may still wait on network calls, connection setup, locks, permission checks, formatting, or sending a large response. Measuring each stage separately shows whether the database remains the main delay. A faster query is useful, but it does not guarantee a fast end-to-end request.
What measurement separates database waiting from the other waiting? Is timing the entire request enough, or does the application need to mark when it sends the search and receives the rows back?

Timing the whole request gives only the total. Add separate measurements around the database call, other external calls, and response construction. Database-side execution timing can then distinguish server work from connection or transfer delay. Compare those measurements using the same request and data; otherwise caching or changing load can make unrelated runs look meaningfully different.

Since A B-tree index guarantees constant-time equality and range filters by locating every relevant key with a single comparison, I figure larger tables should take the same time for these filters. What reason would there be to choose a different index?

What is the practical difference between giving the database more memory and adding an index? They seem equivalent to me because both let it keep information close by instead of reading slowly from the main table.

They solve different problems. More memory lets the database cache frequently used table and index pages, reducing disk reads. An index creates an organized route to particular rows, reducing how much data must be examined. A cached full table can still require checking every row, while an index can narrow the work even when its pages must first be read from storage.

If the whole table already fits in memory, why can a lookup still improve after an index is added? I assumed avoiding the disk removed the slow part, so scanning information that is already loaded should be basically immediate.

Memory removes much of the storage delay, but it does not remove the work of examining rows, evaluating conditions, and moving data through the processor. An index can shrink millions of comparisons to a short navigation plus a few matches. For tiny tables the difference may be negligible, but fitting in memory does not make a full scan free.

Given that Indexes speed many reads without affecting writes because inserts, updates, and deletes modify only the underlying table rows, would it make sense to add more indexes whenever reads need to be faster, or is there a point where additional indexes stop improving reads?

Why does counting all active accounts stay slow after I index the active flag? I was certain an index speeds every query, and this one seems especially simple because the answer depends on only one column.

An index is less helpful when a value appears in a large part of the table. If most accounts are active, the database may still need to visit many index entries and possibly many table rows. Reading the table in one pass can be cheaper. The simplicity of the condition does not determine the amount of data that must be processed.
What does it mean when people say an index has poor variety? Is the problem that many entries point to the same value, or that the database cannot tell which matching account I wanted?

Poor variety usually means the indexed column has few distinct values compared with the number of rows. The database can identify every matching account correctly; accuracy is not the issue. The problem is that one value may lead to a huge set of rows, so the shortcut eliminates little work. Such an index can still help for a rare value.

Since A composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by B equally well because column order is irrelevant, I figure the same index can serve either column on its own. Would adding another index just for B provide any benefit, or would it duplicate what is already available?

What makes later pages of a results list slower than the first page? I assumed an index would make every query equally quick, but asking the database to skip the first ten thousand matches seems to change the wait.

With offset-based paging, the database often still finds and walks past all earlier matching entries before returning the requested page. An index can keep that walk organized, but it cannot necessarily jump over the discarded work for free. Keyset paging avoids this by asking for rows after the last seen key, giving the index a precise place to resume.
Why does the database need to walk past rows it will not send back? Could it divide the page number by the page size and jump straight to that spot, like moving a scrollbar?

Rows are not fixed, interchangeable slots: visibility rules, deleted entries, filters, and ties in the ordering all affect which rows count. An offset describes how many qualifying results to discard, so those results generally must be identified first. A saved boundary value, such as the last timestamp and ID, gives a searchable destination that a page number alone does not.

Given that A covering index contains every row in physical table order, permitting execution without filtering or sorting for any query, I figure every query can rely on the covering index alone. Is there any situation where a query still needs to examine table rows or arrange the result?

Why can a join remain slow when both tables already have indexes? I thought indexes speed every query, so matching customer numbers between two shortcut lists should avoid reading much of either table.

Indexes help a join only when they support the columns and access pattern involved. The database may still process many matching rows, convert mismatched data types, or choose a hash or merge strategy that reads broadly. Returning wide records also adds table lookups. The useful question is not whether both tables have indexes, but whether the chosen plan reduces total work.
What is a join strategy in ordinary terms? Is it just the order in which the database opens the two tables, or does it also change how the matching customer numbers are compared?

It is the method used to pair rows, including which input is handled first and how matches are found. One method repeatedly looks up each key in the other input; another builds an in-memory lookup table; another walks two ordered inputs together. Table size, available indexes, memory, and expected matches influence which method costs least.

Since for a filter matching most rows, an index scan costs less because indexes remain faster at every selectivity, I figure an index scan is always the lower-cost choice. How should someone choose among several indexes for the same filter?

Why does an index become large enough to matter? I pictured it as a small list of pointers, and I believe adding one always speeds searches without changing how much information the database has to carry around.

An index stores a value for each indexed row, a row reference, and structural information that keeps entries searchable. Long values and large tables can therefore produce large indexes. Those pages consume storage and cache space, and reading them has a cost. An index pays off only when its organization saves more work than maintaining and navigating that extra structure requires.
What does it mean for an index to push useful table information out of memory? I assumed the database could simply leave the index on disk until a search needed it and keep the main data loaded.

The database caches whichever pages are being used, whether they belong to tables or indexes. Frequently accessed index pages compete with table pages for a limited cache. It can load an index on demand, but doing so may evict something else, and later reads may reload that displaced data. More indexes can therefore change the overall cache pattern even when each is individually useful.

Given that without a matching expression index, filtering on LOWER(name) uses a conventional index that automatically derives transformed name values, I figure an added expression index repeats work already being done. When is creating one still useful?

Why is the first run of a search often slower than repeating the same search? I take that to mean extra memory is effectively doing the same job as an index once the database has remembered the table.

The first run may load table or index pages from storage and initialize other resources; later runs can reuse cached pages. That makes the same route faster, but it does not create the organized lookup path an index provides. A warm full scan still examines the relevant table pages, whereas a suitable index may let the database avoid most of them.
What exactly is remembered after that first search? Is the database keeping the answer somewhere, or is it only keeping chunks of the table so it can repeat the same work more quickly?

Usually it is the underlying data and index pages that remain in memory, not the final answer. The database still executes the query and checks visibility and conditions again. Some systems or surrounding applications have result caches, but that is a separate feature. This distinction matters because changed rows and differently worded searches can reuse pages without reusing an old answer.

Since Query planners derive exact row counts directly from SQL text, so stale table and index statistics cannot affect execution plans, I figure refreshing those statistics has no effect on a plan. Why keep the statistics at all, and what purpose do they serve?

What happens when an indexed column contains lots of repeated values, such as a country name? I believe the index still speeds every query because it groups matching entries together, even if one group contains nearly the whole table.

Grouping helps locate the start of the matches, but the database must still process the entries in that group. If a country contains most rows, using the index may require many scattered table lookups, which can cost more than reading the table steadily. The index is more valuable for uncommon countries because it lets the database skip a larger share of data.
Why are scattered lookups slower than reading the table steadily? If all the needed pieces are on the same drive, I would expect the amount of information read to be the only thing that matters.

Access pattern matters as well as total bytes. A steady scan reads neighboring pages efficiently and processes them in batches. Index entries may point to table rows spread across many pages, causing extra page visits and less predictable access. Caching and solid-state storage reduce that difference, but they do not erase the additional bookkeeping or repeated page handling.

Given that Any index on the queried table avoids a separate sort, regardless of its indexed columns or key order, I figure one existing index is enough whenever sorted results are needed. What reason is there to add another index for a different key order?

Why can searching a customer number be slow when the number column already has an index? I assumed indexes speed every query, but this search compares a typed-in number with values that the table stores as text.

The different data types can force a conversion before comparison. Depending on which side is converted and how the database handles it, the stored text values may no longer match the index's organized form. Using matching parameter and column types usually avoids that obstacle. The index is not broken; the comparison may simply be asking for a different operation.
What does matching the types mean in practice? Should the application send the customer number as text, or should the table column be changed so the database treats every stored value as a number?

Use the type that represents the data correctly. If customer numbers can contain leading zeros, letters, or formatting, text may be appropriate, and the application should send text parameters. If they are truly quantities, a numeric type may fit. Changing the column requires checking existing values and dependent code; matching the parameter is usually the smaller immediate correction.

Since A B-tree index accelerates selective equality and range filters by locating relevant keys without scanning every table row, I figure it is most useful when a filter matches only a small share of rows. How does the benefit change as that share grows?
What happens when I search for rows where a field is blank? I believe an index on that field speeds every query, yet the database sometimes reads the full table when I ask for missing values.

Blank can mean an empty value or a null marker, and databases treat those differently. Some index types or systems omit nulls, while others store them. Even when nulls are indexed, a scan may be cheaper if most rows are missing that value. First confirm what the data contains, then inspect whether the index can represent and efficiently narrow that condition.
Why would a shortcut list leave missing values out? I assumed every table row received an entry, even when the entry only said that nothing had been filled in for that field.

Omitting nulls can make an index smaller and reflects the fact that null means an unknown or absent value rather than an ordinary value. This behavior is specific to the database and index definition, so it should not be assumed universally. If searches for missing values matter, the system may support an index designed specifically for rows meeting that condition.

Given that Indexes speed many reads but add storage and write overhead because inserts, updates, and deletes also modify index structures, how should I decide when faster reads justify adding another index?

Why does searching through linked tables sometimes get faster after indexing a reference number? I had assumed adding RAM was the same as adding an index, because either one should keep those links ready for quick use.

Memory can keep pages close to the processor, but it does not arrange reference numbers for direct lookup. An index does that organization, letting the database find related rows without checking every cached row. For joins, an index on the referencing column can be particularly useful when only a small set of parent records is involved. More RAM and indexing can complement each other.
What is the referencing column in that situation? Is it the number stored on the child record, or the original number on the parent record that the child is pointing toward?

The referencing column is on the child side: it stores a value that points to a key on the parent. The parent's key is the referenced column and is commonly indexed by a primary-key or unique constraint. Indexing the child column can speed finding all children for one parent; the relationship rule itself does not always create that child-side index.

Since A composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by A because A is its leading column, I figure a separate index on A repeats the same support. When is the separate index still useful?

Why does searching for a word in the middle of a description stay slow after the description is indexed? I thought an index makes every kind of search faster, including words that appear anywhere inside a longer piece of text.

A conventional ordered index is arranged from the beginning of each stored value, so it can often help with exact matches or known prefixes. A search for text anywhere in the middle lacks that starting point and may inspect many values. Specialized full-text, trigram, or other text-search indexes organize content differently and can support that pattern more effectively.
What is the shortcut list storing for a long description? Does it keep a second full copy of every sentence in sorted order, or only a pointer and a shortened version of the text?

That depends on the database and index type. A basic ordered index generally stores the indexed value, or an encoded form of it, together with a row reference and structural metadata. It can therefore duplicate substantial text and may face size limits. A full-text index instead stores terms and references in a structure designed for word searches, not simply sorted sentences.

Given that A covering index contains every column needed by a query, permitting execution without extra row lookups in the base table, I figure it can answer that query from the index alone. What changes to the query would prevent that benefit?
